FAILURE OF BOILERS IN CENTRAL HEATING PLANT
speechtext:
I consider it my duty to inform the house that this morning I received many calls from hon. members complaining of the temperature in this building. Some hon. members suggested to me that under the prevailing conditions there should be no sitting of the house this afternoon. Hon. members will realize that it is for the house itself to decide whether we should sit or not.
I communicated with those who are responsible for the heating of the building and was informed that there had been an accident in the central heating plant, but they hoped that sometime about noon or one o'clock today they would be able to send some steam into the chamber. Just before coming into the house at three o'clock I was told that unfortunately the repairs had not yet been made, and that it would be impossible to heat the building this afternoon. I thought it my duty therefore to bring the facts to the attention of the house. The temperature in this chamber is now about 64 degrees, and in some parts of the building it is only 60.
I thought that before we proceeded with the business of the house hon. members would like to know these facts so that the house might decide whether there should be a sitting this afternoon. Those who have been complaining about the temperature cannot expect any improvement this afternoon.

maintopic: FAILURE OF BOILERS IN CENTRAL HEATING PLANT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I suggest that it ivould be well if we could have our sittings in Vancouver?

speakeroldname: Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works):
maintopic: FAILURE OF BOILERS IN CENTRAL HEATING PLANT
speechtext:
Before the house comes to a hast.% decision as to whether we should sit or not, I should like to make the following statement.
On account of the unduly severe weather that has prevailed during the present week it
was necessary to force the capacity of the plant to the extreme limit, and under such circumstances one boiler failed. The central heating plant is composed of six boilers, all of which are connected to a central manifold, and they have been used and have met the demands imposed upon them even with the additional temporary construction that was put up during wartime. One boiler failed in a minor way at midnight on the 9th, and it was necessary to close this one down to make repairs. While these repairs were under way, the other five boilers were under additional pressure and the second boiler failed after midnight. Both repairs are not what might be considered serious. They can be corrected temporarily, and it is hoped that one boiler will be back on the line in an hour or so, and the other one will be ready by tomorrow morning.
These are circumstances over which we have little or no control as they are brought about by reason of severe weather. While the plant is overhauled between heating seasons, it is found that today the scarcity of materials makes it difficult to replace with new parts the wear and tear that has ordinarily taken place; and, in substitution, wear and tear has been replaced by welding and other processes to tide over until such time as it is possible to make adequate renewals.
At present we have working on the building the Campbell Steel and Iron Works and the staff of the public works department. The last information I received was that during the afternoon we shall have the ordinary temperature in the building.

speechtext:
I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. It arises out of the fact that we have on the order paper a bill to amend the Dairy Industry Act with regard to oleomargarine. My question is this. Did the
Oleomargarine

government in signing the Geneva trade agreements agree to remove the embargo against the importation of oleomargarine?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REMOVAL OF EMBARGO UNDER GENEVA AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has been giving special attention to the situation that arises with regard to oleomargarine under the agreements. I would suggest that my colleague reply.
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): The trade agreements signed1 at Geneva, Mr. Speaker, are being applied provisionally between Canada and the signatories of the protocol of provisional application which is printed1 at page 85 of our document, treaty series 1947, No. 27.
Under that protocol, the signatories are applying parts 1 and 3 of the general agreement on tariffs and trade and they are required to apply part 2 only to an extent not inconsistent with existing legislation.
Articles XI and XX of the general agreement are those which deal with the exclusion of prohibitions or restrictions other than duties; they are both in part 2 and there is no obligation to apply them in any way that would require now the modification of existing legislation.
The general agreement itself will not come into force in such manner as to make part 2 a requirement that any signatory modify existing legislation until the thirtieth day following the day on which instruments of acceptance have 'been deposited with the secretary general of the united nations on behalf of governments signatory to the Final Act, the territories of which account for 85 per centum of the total external trade of the territories of the signatories to the Final Act as provided in article XXVI, subsection 5, of the general agreement.
There are twenty-three signatories to that Final Act, and the percentage shares of total external trade to be used under article XXVI to determine when you reach the 85 per cent is stated in annex A-H, which is printed at page 76 of our publication.
It is apt to be some months yet before the requirements of article XXVI for the coming into force of the general agreement shall have been satisfied.
The signatories of the protocol of provisional application are:	Australia, Belgium-
Luxembourg-Netherlands, Canada, Cuba, France, United Kingdom and United States. They are extending to each other the benefits of the concessions negotiated between them respectively and some of them are even extending to each other the benefits of con-

cessions negotiated with countries whose governments have not yet signed the protocol, but they are not bound to do so, and we ourselves have excluded from the provisional application the concessions we negotiated with Norway because Norway has not yet signed the protocol. This was done by order in council P.C. 5270 of December 23, 1947.
The question of the effect of articles XI and XX of the general trade agreement, when it does become binding on the signatories, is now being considered by the Department of Justice. Hon. members will see that the general exclusion of prohibitions or restrictions other than tariff charges or tariff duties is followed by paragraph 2 which declares that those provisions do not apply in certain cases. The effect of the exceptions on such legislation as exists in Canada that would amount to prohibitions is being considered at the present time by the Department of Justice.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REMOVAL OF EMBARGO UNDER GENEVA AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Perhaps the minister
would permit one other question. From his answer are we to understand that at the moment we are not in the position of having agreed to remove this embargo? And further are we to understand that the minister is not in a position now to say what the final effect of the signing of these agreements is with regard to the embargo on oleomargarine? Is that a correct interpretation of what the minister had to say?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I would prefer to put it this way. An agreement has been signed which has not yet come into force. Certain portions of it are being applied under a protocol of provisional application. None of the things which are required by the protocol of provisional application makes it necessary for us to modify any of our legislation. The Department of Justice is studying the question whether, when it does come into effect, the general trade agreement would require us to modify the Dairy Industry Act which deals with oleomargarine or certain tariff provisions which exclude secondhand machinery or commodities. These questions are being studied at the present time by the Department of Justice.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REMOVAL OF EMBARGO UNDER GENEVA AGREEMENTS

Mr. ST. LAURENT:	The government
knows that articles XI and XX are the general rules which will apply, but there are exceptions. It is a question on which the government will have to act on its responsi-

Under the statute, it will then have to say whether or not it considers that the exceptions affect this provision of the Dairy Industry Act and the provision about the exclusion of secondhand commodities, unless there is agreement to modify these exceptions.
Just a week ago today I had an interesting conversation with our chief representative at the Havana conference, and these two articles are still being debated at Havana. speechtext:
1.	Have any plans been made by the Department of Labour or any other federal department to call a conference for the purpose of discussing the welfare and rehabilitation of handicapped persons in Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: CONFERENCE ON WELFARE AND REHABILITATION OF HANDICAPPED PERSONS
speechtext:
1 and 2. On 26th August, 1947, committee of privy council, on my recommendation, approved order in council P.C. 2961 granting permission for the Department of Labour to hold a national conference to consider the vocational rehabilitation of physically handicapped persons. Under the terms of this order in council the conference was to be attended by delegates nominated by private organizations working on behalf of physically handicapped, as well as representatives of the dominion and provincial governments.
The order in council set the dates for the conference in the month of October but plans could not be completed and it was necessary to defer arrangements for the conference until
Orders for Returns

December. In view of the decision to call parliament into session on December 5, it was again considered necessary to postpone the conference as it was felt that many of those persons interested in vocational rehabilitation of physically handicapped persons would not be able to devote sufficient time to the conference while parliament is in session.
In the meantime, officials of various branches of the Department of Labour are continuing to study the matter of vocational rehabilitation of disabled persons.

CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Was that a correct statement?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I do not know; but I know this-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Do you question the accuracy of it?

The Address-Mr. Gillis

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I do not know anything about it. But if it is on a par with the statement issued by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, then it leaves a question in my mind whether it will relieve the situation which I know exists down there.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You know nothing whatever about it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
And I do not think you know much about it, either.
I have in my hand a further clipping with respect to the longshoremen's union, which presides over the wages and destiny of men employed on the waterfront. In fact in the final analysis they keep that city going; they are the wage earners. They say: "Worst in twenty years; nothing being done; no immediate solution."
I have another clipping from Halifax, dated February 6, headed "Unemployed now need assistance," and stating that Halifax has 4,500 jobless who may ask their provincial and civic governments that unemployment relief be instituted immediately. That statement is issued by the director of the workers' federation at that point. I have read press dispatches emanating from Halifax and I do not believe any good purpose is served for the people in that part of the country if the rest of the people of Canada are asked to believe that things are fine down there, and that there is nothing wrong. I know they are not fine. They leave much to be desired. Something has to be done in that part of the country, and done very soon, if those people are to continue to support our present institutions. They are getting anything but a square deal from us.
The point I am making is that the unemployment situation prevailing in that part of Canada today is not new. The fact of the matter is it was anticipated in 1942. The senior member for Halifax was a member of the reconstruction committee.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: A good member.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am not saying anything about that; I leave that for you to say. All members are good; they do the best they can, with whatever little ability God gave them- and some have not much. I said it was anticipated by that committee, and that the committee was a good one. It was a fact-finding committee like the one on prices. It will go out with a miner's rod looking for profiteers. That committee was a good one and I enjoyed working on it. I think it really did a job because it dug out a lot of facts and served many industries. The committee came back to this house and made a report. It had the power to recommend, something the present
prices committee has not got; it is set up merely to gather something which will collect dust in the archives.
The Journals of the House of Commons, 1943-44, contain the recommendations of that committee on the subject I am talking about now. I want to put those recommendations on the record, in order to show that the unemployment situation now prevailing in the maritimes was anticipated by the government and acted upon by that reconstruction committee. I should like to quote from the recommendations of the committee with respect to the maritimes, to be found on page 723 as follows:
This inquiry should include the extent, if any, to which the maritimes have suffered because of lack of proper distribution of secondary industry in Canada, and also the possibility of securing extended markets-both Canadian and international-for all maritime production.
They were recommending an inquiry into the whole situation which prevailed in that end of the country. The report continues:
We are convinced that after the war-if prewar conditions are permitted to prevail-the Nova Scotia coal industry will not be able to exist without assistance in the marketing of the output of the mines. The coal industry situation would, therefore, be an important part of the proposed survey.
After the war, transportation will play an even more important part than previously in economic development.
Therefore in dealing noth conditions in the maritime provinces, we strongly urge that the government give earnest consideration to certain proposed improvements in transportation facilities. These include:
(a)	Improvements designed to make communications between Prince Edward Island and the mainland constant, reliable and adequate.
(b)	Improvement of transportation across the strait of Canso by the construction of a cause-wav. or in such manner as may be judged most satisfactory, considering the amount of traffic and the conditions of ice, tides and current.
(c)	Regrading, realigning and double-tracking of the Canadian National railway from Sydney to points in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
I was in on all the discussions leading up to that recommendation. It was estimated that if the government undertook that particular project it would give employment to 7,000 people for at least four years. Had that one recommendation in connection with Nova Scotia been carried out by the government we would not be reading the headlines about unemployment that we are seeing today in the press all across the country. It would have settled the problem of employment for at least four years.
In the meantime the governments, provincial and federal, have had an opportunity to carry on a survey of secondary industries as was recommended by that reconstruction com-
The Address-Mr. Gillis

mittee. Absolutely nothing has been done about this except that the Minister of Transport has done some boring and he knows how deep the water is. I am glad he is to follow me, because then I will have an official answer to the questions I am asking. That govem-mentndominated committee recommended unanimously what should be done, but it has not been done. I should like to give hon. members a little more information.
I have talked about this to some hon. members from Ontario. They have said to me, "Well, $20,000,000 or $26,000,000 is a lot of money to spend to build a bridge from the island of Cape Breton to the mainland of Nova Scotia." I was talking to one fellow about this problem of unemployment and when I reached the strait of Canso and started across he said, "Wait a minute; you are not in Canada." I said, "No? Where am I?" He said, "You are on the way to Newfoundland." I showed him the map and was able to convince him that we are still part of Canada. It is not a wilderness down there. Perhaps I had better give the house the opinion of the board of trade, because if I said this hon. members might not believe me; they might think it was just propaganda.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why should we believe the board of trade?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
They are nice fellows and
they are non-political. They give a description of the island and state that it is the most important industrial centre east of Montreal. This report continues:
Cape Breton is an island forming the northeast part of Nova Scotia, jutting out into the Atlantic and separated from the rest of Canada by the narrow strait of Canso. With a land area of 3,120 square miles and a population of 200,000 (1945 estimate), it is the most concentrated industrial area east -of Montreal. The key industries are coal, steel, tourism, lumber, fishing and farming. It is significant that one-third of Canada's coal output and one-quarter of its pig iron comes from Gape Breton. Being closest geographically to Newfoundland and the continent, its fine harbours handle large amounts of exports and imports through the Sydneys_ and Louisburg.
There are some people living there and this island means something economically to the rest of Canada. I have here an editorial from the Sydney Post-Record, which is not a C.C.F. paper. I am sure my hon. friends from Cape Breton will agree with me when I say that. I think myself the engineering branch of the Department of Transport should get down to brass tacks and make a better guess, and I say "guess" advisedly. The first survey for this bridge was made in 1906 by Waddell Mardestry Company of New York, a well

known engineering firm. The report they made at that time was made available to the reconstruction committee. According to them it was a feasible project. Of course their estimate of that time would have to be revised considerably, but even so it would not be in accordance with the figures the department are giving out at the present time. This editorial reads:
Mr. MacLachlan said a causeway would cost between $10,000,000 and $12,000,000, a steel and concrete bridge between $15,000,000 and $20,000,000. In a subsequent report to the government, which was babied in the house last spring, .Mr. MacLachlan's estimates were briskly stepped up to $32,000,000 for -the causeway and $54,000,000 for the -bridge. Obviously Mr. MacLachlan has been doing more guessing than figuring, and he seems capable -at any time of producing the kind of estimates he thinks his principals or his audiences, as the case may be, -would like him to produce. In the circumstances, an independent inquiry is what the needs of the case clearly indicate.
That is merely a press dispatch, but I have here a return which was tabled by the minister on April 23, 1947. It was stated at that time that a causeway would cost $17,797,000 and a bridge, $26,275,000. All kinds of figures have been thrown around. I have another report to which I should like to make reference, because I consider this man is qualified to talk on the subject. The caption is "Bridge over the strait of Canso." I do not know whether the minister has read this -article.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I have read it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Then there is no need for me to read it again. The minister agrees with it?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I have not said that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The article is by Charles P. Disney, consulting engineer, Toronto, and retired engineer of bridges, Canadian National Railways. I am sure they would not employ anybody who was featherheaded or incompetent. This gentleman says on page 4:
Chief of these is -the fact that the bridge would eliminate -the very costly ferries -and -terminals that nun7 provide the only means of access to and egress from the island, particularly the t-rain ferries of the Canadian National Railways which involve in the neighbourhood of a million-dollars-a-year maintenance charge for the ferries and the slips and terminal facilities on either side. The saving through the abolition of two complete terminals with their rail-road maintenance and operating equipment and personnel, plus the elimination of the necessity of rebuilding or replacing the present worn-out and obsolete ferries at a cost of millions of dollars, would go a long way towards paying the cost of the bridge.
I was rather disturbed when it was brought to my attention that the government were building another ferry for use at that point at a cost of $5,000,000.

The Address-Mr. Gillis

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Surely not anything like that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The hon. gentleman was in the house when the statement was made.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, I was not.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My recollection is that he was.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My recollection is seeing the statement first in the press that it would cost $5,000,000 and maintenance charges of $l,000j000 a year. If a bridge were built it would pay for itself in a few years. Ferries are an obsolete means of transportation, no matter what kind of ferry it may be, and you will have exactly the same kind of bottleneck you have now. It will not improve conditions at all. I cannot understand the thinking of people who recommend that kind of thing when the construction of a bridge is the modern thing and would lead to the expansion of industry at both ends. One of the main reasons why there is not more secondary industry in that part of the country is the lack of transportation facilities. A bridge would encourage the development of industry and be in keeping with modern life. I would rather walk than take that old train that sputters along over an old roadbed and takes fifteen hours to go from Halifax to Cape Breton. But it does not look as if the government has any intention of building a bridge, having made this large expenditure of $5,000,000 in perpetuating an obsolete means of transportation by ferry.
This man Disney makes a very sensible report. He points out that he has had objections from people in Ontario and Quebec that the government of Canada should not be expected to make such a large expenditure in that part of the country, a charge on all the taxpayers of the country. But Mr. Disney points out that this is no local project; it is a national project.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It has support from Ontario too.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Definitely, and I am glad to hear that from the hon. member for Peel. A large part of the personnel that would be employed in the construction of a bridge at that point would come from this part of the country, and a large part of the materials used. Most of the steel would be rolled here and shipped down there. It would mean something for practically every part of this country, and the project should therefore not be considered a merely local one. Mr. Disney
comments on that in his report and I merely mention it now to dispose of that parochial angle. It is not something which the people in that part of the country are just hollering for. We are entitled to it. If there was such a bottleneck in Ontario or Quebec it would be cured and cured very quickly without any quibbling, but this Canso question has been a matter of controversy and investigation since 1906 and the controversy is still going on. However the Minister of Transport is both aggressive and progressive, and I am in hopes that the controversy will not last much longer.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
He must be going to do something about it.
Mr. Disney also points out that there is a certain kind of pier being put down now- I shall not go into the technical details because the minister knows the kind of pier I mean-which could be used there. Already a bridge has been built in the province of Quebec, across deep water, with a greater span, where there is just as much tide as there is in the strait of Canso, and that bridge is standing up.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And there is another one at St. Catharines, Ontario.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, and one in Quebec province too. I understand that they offered to build a sample pier in the centre of the channel and let it remain there to demonstrate that that type of pier will stand up against the tides and ice, which are the conditions on which the department base their objections to the building of a bridge. I would suggest that the minister read the whole report, because I cannot accept the departmental estimate that it would cost $54,000,000 to construct a bridge across the strait of Canso. I am inclined to accept Mr. Disney's estimate of $20,000,000 more or less. I think that is nearer the mark, although it may be a little low, but I shall not comment further on that.
I would point out to the minister that another investigation is being carried on. Boring has been going on since 1945 and all that part of the work is now done. The examination of costs is not yet completed. A board of engineers has been selected in consultation between the Premier of Nova Scotia and the federal government. I presume that negotiations were carried on through the Minister of Transport; and that board is going to make a survey of transportation facilities.
The Address-Mr. Gillis

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Does my hon. friend object to the establishment of that board?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am going to object to it in a moment. The establishment of transportation facilities-what does that mean? It means, is the old ferry good, bad or indifferent? That is the proposed investigation, and you do not have to investigate that. You need only ask me. I have often gone over in the ferry, as I think the minister has himself, and it is about the worst transportation on the North American continent. Now that you have the provincial government co-operating -I think the gesture of the federal government was a very anaemic one-the board of engineers should determine the feasibility of that causeway or bridge and what the cost would be.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is exactly what thejr are going to do.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Is it? The press dispatch said that the board would examine transportation facilities, and I visualized their looking over the old ferry to see whether it went fast or slow.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Often press reports are away out of line.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is right. I am glad that the minister has clarified that point and says that the board are going to determine the feasibility of the project, the cost and so forth.
My objection to that board of engineers is this. The three men appointed are from Quebec and Ontario. They are Professor D. S. Ellis, dean of engineering at Queen's university, Kingston; Doctor Arthur Surveyer, and Doctor P. L. Pratley, both Montreal consulting engineers.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Are you objecting to the board of engineers?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes. I am still objecting and I am objecting for this reason. I do not think the minister had to go outside the house. He has an engineer sitting behind him. He has the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Revenue, the member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Winters), and there are several others in this house who are qualified to go there and do that kind of job.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why don't you and the minister go down yourselves?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He has engineers in Nova Scotia.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What about the member for Davenport?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am not being political about this. I do not want any opposition member to go. My conception of engineers is that they are practical fellows who are loyal to their profession and they do not like to let the profession down in such matters. I would be satisfied with the member for Queens-Lunen-burg. He has a great deal of ability in that field. But someone definitely interested, someone living in that part of the country, should have been included as a member of the board. Professors who are teaching in universities are secure in a world of books, and with all due respect to their profession I think that someone in the sticks who is living outside and is doing that kind of work should be on the board.
I am not going to exceed my time. I merely want to conclude by saying this. There was a time when the maritime provinces were quite in the minority and would be outvoted no matter whether they co-operated one hundred per cent or not. At the present time, if the maritime province members banded together in the interests of that part of the country they could force any vote they wanted to through this house. The present government has twelve of a majority. There are twenty-six maritime members here, and if we got together on that causeway and said, "No vote for your committee unless you make the commitment that you will give us that causeway"-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: A threat of blackmail.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The whole system under which you live is blackmail. That is merely exercising your legitimate prerogative to get something done for the part of the country you represent, and I say that we could force the implementation of the report of a committee on which the government had a majority. If we got together and forced the implementation of that report, it would create employment and link up that part of the country with the rest of Canada. It would give that part of the country a half decent break, and that would be only doing our duty to the people we represent. British Columbia, I am sure, would do it. When it is a question of apples or lumber, of Japanese or fisheries, you generally find the British Columbia members, whether Liberals, Tories or C.C.F'ers, fairly well united on the subject.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not on the Japanese.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am suggesting to the members from the maritime provinces that on this particular subject we should try to get together to get something done. We should

The Address-Mr. Chevrier
have secondary industries there. We should have that causeway, and there are several other things we should have.
When the Minister of Trade and Commerce was in Halifax recently he gave a press interview. He was asked whether it was not possible for the members from the maritime provinces to get together and force something along the lines I have suggested. The minister's answer was, "What are they asking for that they are not getting done?" The implication there is that we are not asking for anything, because we are not getting anything done. I think we should accept that challenge, and any time the senior member for Halifax is ready to call a caucus on maritime projects, for the purpose of getting together and forcing some recognition of that part of the country, he can give me a buzz and I shall be glad to join him.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If I rise to take part in the debate it is not so much to reply to the hon. member for Cape Breton South, (Mr. Gillis) as it is to deal with two matters which concern the Canadian National Railways and the pension fund of the railways. Before embarking on these two matters, however, I think it is in order that I should say a word or two in reply to some of the statements that have been made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
In concluding his remarks the hon. gentleman said that the members from the mari-times evidently had not asked for very much since they had received very little. Apparently my hon. friend's memory is quite short. He must have forgotten that within a very short period of time the government had spent, from 1936 until 1946, no less than
818,000,000 in the maritime provinces, and at the moment they have a program concerning the harbours of Saint John and Halifax which will cost no less than $8,000,00. So that when the hon. gentleman said they had asked for nothing and had received nothing-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not yet.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: -he was unquestionably wrong.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Merely promises.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The senior member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor), in a statement he made the other day, referred to some of the expenditure that was about to be made in the port of Halifax, and he was correct in the statement he made. I have not seen it, but I have heard it quoted by the hon. member for Cape Breton South.

The hon. member for Lake Centre referred to the Canadian National Railways' pension fund, and he quoted rule 12 which I, too, should like to put on Hansard. Rule 12 reads as follows:
Every employee who joins the service of the company hereafter before attaining the age of 45 years shall, if he remains continuously in the company's service to age 65, be entitled to receive upon his retirement a basic pension of $3'00 per annum, which amount shall be provided at the sole expense of the company.
This rule entitles the employee upon retirement to a minimum pension of $25 a month, which is paid at the sole expense of the company. No contribution is required as in most pension plans. This is the first or basic plan of the Canadian National Railways, and in effect it is in recognition of the ten years of service by the employees of the company. But this is only part of the story. The hon. member for Lake Centre did not put on the record rule 22, which should be read in conjunction with rule 12. I should like to place on Hansard rule 22, which reads as follows:
Upon retirement each employee shall receive such basic pension or service pension as he maybe entitled to under this pension fund. He will, in addition, receive such supplemental annuity as may be purchasable from the company by the amount of his contributions added to the contributions credited by the company together with accrued interest compounded thereon.
If an employee exercises his right to contribute to t'he fund after completion of ten years' service, which contribution may be from one to ten per cent of his salary, the company will contribute a like amount up to five per cent. These contributions by the employee and the company with compound interest to date of the employee's retirement will result in a considerable supplemental annuity, and the total amount of the pension together with the basic pension paid at the sole expense of the company will be a substantial amount added to his salary.
Let me take an example of this. Let us assume that an employee at age twenty-five begins to work for the Canadian National Railways and has a continuing period of employment of forty years. Let us assume that during that forty years' time he receives S100 a month. He may contribute from one to ten per cent of his salary. Let us assume that his contribution is five per cent of his salary. That five per cent is matched by the railway; and that means in effect that he will be receiving a monthly straight life pension which will be in excess of S75 a month. There are, of course, some employees who are in the low brackets and who majr not be able to contribute one to five per cent or who may 5849-72J
not be able to contribute anything at all. However, the pension plan is drawn up in such a way that they may contribute; they have an opportunity to do so, and the failure of an employee to take advantage of the privilege to contribute cannot be charged against the Canadian National Railways. The total contracts issued under this plan number 11,617, of which 9,595 are still in force. Most pension plans provide for contributions by the employees, including employees in the low-wage brackets. In the case of the Canadian National Railways plan, this is purely voluntary; therefore the Canadian National minimum cannot be judged without consideration to the other features of the plan. The second and, I think, more important matter with which I should like to deal was brought up by the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Hazen), who complained bitterly that the export rate on eight or ten commodities to the port of Portland, Maine, had been reduced. He charged that the traditional and historic policy of the government and of Canada, to encourage trade and traffic through its own Canadian ports, had been violated. The hon. gentleman based his whole argument upon a false premise and' upon facts which at times were inaccurate. His charges against the officers of the Canadian National Railways were wholly and entirely unwarranted. .
My first words, Mr. Speaker, will be to assure the house that I, as Minister of Transport, and the government of Canada did not depart one iota from the traditional policy of encouraging traffic through Canadian ports. In fact I expect to be able to establish that positive action to encourage the use of our ports and to assist in the betterment of the facilities of those ports has been and will continue to be taken. The hon. member based his remarks upon two things that had occurred. The first was the action of the Canadian National Railways in equalizing the rates to Portland on eight or ten commodities, and the consequent withdrawal or shifting of the sailings of the Moore-McCormack Lines, a United States concern, from the ports of Saint John and Halifax to the port of Portland. The second was the routing of a million bushels of rye by the French supply council through Portland instead of through a Canadian port. The hon. member dwelt at great length on the traditional policy of Canada, and quoted statements made from time to

time by public men, former premiers of New Brunswick and former prime ministers of the dominion. As far as those statements are concerned, I find myself in entire agreement with my hon. friend; but from that point on we must part company. I want to refer to the Canadian Northern Railway Act of 1911, and I should like to quote section 13. I refer to that act particularly, because it contains in essence what parliament intended the policy of Canada and of the railways should be:
The company must agree (1) that all freight originating on its lines, not specifically routed otherwise, shall when destined for points in Canada be carried over the railways within Canada; (2) that the through rates on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports; (3) that all such traffic not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper shall be carried to Canadian ports; and (4) that the companies shall not in any matter within their powers directly or indirectly advise or encourage the transportation of such freight by routes other than those above provided, but shall in all respects, in good faith, use their utmost endeavours to fulfil its conditions upon which public aid is granted, namely, the development of trade through Canadian channels and Canadian ocean ports.
My contention is that nothing done by the Canadian government or nothing done by the Canadian 'National Railways in any way viol-lated the traditional policy as laid down in that and other statute law in this parliament.
Since the hon. member claims that this policy has been violated, it becomes necessary for me to bring to the house the facts which arose in connection with this incident. What are the facts? They are as follows: Since 1905 the export rate on all commodities moving east of Kingston through the three ports of Halifax, Saint John and Portland have been on a parity, with but one exception, namely, that Saint John had an advantage of one cent per 100 pounds over the port of Halifax until 1923, when the Canadian National Railways system was set up and established; and it was the Canadian National Railways which did away with the one cent per 100 pounds preference in favour of Saint John.
From that time on, until 1938, the three ports remained on a parity. In 1938 the interstate commerce commission of the United States granted a ten per cent increase on export rates to the port of Portland. In the same year, or shortly after the United States application, a similar application was made to the board of transport commissioners for Canada, asking for a similar increase; and the board of transport commissioners did grant a similar increase of ten per cent and again placed the three ports on a parity.

The Address-Mr. Chevrier
Because of representations made by various interests to the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian National Railways decided to forgo the ten per cent, not on all the commodities, but on eight or ten only. The remaining rates, which were by far the majority, remained on a parity among the three ports. In November, 1947, the Canadian National Railways equalized the rates to Portland on the remaining eight or ten commodities. In doing this, the traditional policy of the Canadian government, as well as the obligation placed upon the railways of this country, and as laid down in various statute laws, was not in any way violated. No discrimination was exercised against any Canadian port. The only thing that was done was to equalize rates with reference to the three ports, a condition that had existed over many years.
I should now like to deal with the reasons why the rates were equalized by the Canadian National Railways to Portland; and in order to do this I should like to refer to the letter written by Moore-McCormack Lines Incorporated to the Canadian National Railways and to quote two paragraphs therefrom.
First let me remind the house that a shipowner is of course entirely free to arrange his sailings according to what he considers his best interests; and it is not uncommon that shift-ings take place from time to time. The letter I have in my hand states that at least one of the reasons why the shifting from the maritime ports to Portland took place was because of undue time taken at the berth in the winter season of 1946-47 waiting for and loading cargoes.
During that season, as the house knows, not only were the railways of this country hard pressed to bring equipment to the maritime provinces, and in fact, to all parts of Canada, but the weather was such that delays in shipping took place from time to time. Those were conditions over which the railways, and certainly over which the national harbours board had no control.
In September of last year the national harbours board held a conference at Montreal of all interested organizations to review the operations of the previous season at the maritime ports, and to secure co-operative effort for the present season. Committees were established; and I am glad to say at this time, from the information I have received from these ports, that conditions have been materially bettered. In fact our terminals at Saint John and Halifax handled substantially more traffic in December last than in the same month of the previous year.

December 9, 1947.
Mr. F. J. Stock,
Traffic Manager-Foreign Freight Department, Canadian National Railways,
Board of Trade Building,
Montreal, Canada.
Aly dear Mr. Stock,
We beg to confirm our conversation that was held in this office in April of this year, when we complained to you bitterly in consequence of the extremely poor service that had been rendered to our vessels at the winter ports of St. John, N.B., and Halifax, N.S., in the winter of 1946-1947.
At that time we discussed the progress of our Canadian service to the east coast of South America and the plans that we were laying for the future in injecting our fast combination passenger and freight and reefer vessels, when we advised that it would be impossible to do this until better arrangements could be made as to winter service.
We advised you specifically that our first vessel which loaded at Saint John-the Pontus H. Ross-actually arrived at 12.32 p.m. on December 15 and she was delayed in getting a berth and did not start loading until 9.30 a.m. on December 18. She was delayed very greatly in not being able to get her cargo in consequence of the congestion of harbour facilities, with the result that she did not sail until January 18. 1947. having been in the harbour thirty-four days and loaded with some 5,488 tons of cargo.
The Address-Mr. Chevrier

In consequence of this unfortunate operation, we conferred with our agents, Montreal Shipping Company, who recommended that our next vessel be berthed at Halifax, N.S. Accordingly, the Berkeley Victory arrived in Halifax on January 19, and did not commence loading until January 22. She sailed February 2-fourteen days in harbour-and loaded 4,941 tons, all of which by comparison with operations at other ports -was still extremely bad.
Our next vessel was the Vernon S. Hood. She arrived at Halifax on March 4, and did not dock until March 7. Our experience -with this ship was the same as with the other ships, and it was not until March 14 she sailed, and then with a part cargo only, i.e., 3,596 tons, after she had remained in port ten days.
In consequence of these very bad performances, we decided to cancel our April vessel and resume service from Montreal in June. In our conversation with you in April of this year, notwithstanding your urgent reouest that we give the ports of Halifax and 'Saint John a further trial, we had to regretfully advise you that we could not see how7 w7e could resume service at these ports during the winter of 1947-48. Before making this decision final, w7e conferred w7ith the Montreal Shipping Company, w7ho advised that they did not see very much hope for improvement.
With this before us, we appealed to you to make some adjustment in the rates so that the port of Portland. Me., could be used as an overflow7 port until such time as the operations at the ports of Halifax and Saint John were improved so as to provide efficient and economical operation of ships at these ports.
T now7 understand that you have so arranged to equalize the rates to Portland. Me., as against the other ports, and I want to take this opportunity to thank you for your kind co-operation, this from both ourselves and our shippers, w7ho otherwise would have been forced to route their cargoes from Canadian points of shipment via Boston or New York.
Yours faithfully.
Moore-McCormack Lines, Inc.
Where in that letter is there any indication of inducement on the part of the Canadian National Railways to withdraw trade from Canada to the port of Portland? On the contrary, the letter clearly states:
. . . notwithstanding your urgent request that we give the ports of Halifax and Saint John a further trial, we had to regretfully advise you that we could not see how wre could resume service at these ports.
And then there is this part in the last paragraph:
I now understand that you have so arranged to equalize the rates to Portland. Maine, as against the other ports, and I want to take this opportunity to thank you for your kind co-operation, this from both ourselves and our shippers w7ho otherwise would have been forced to route their cargoes from Canadian points of shipment via Boston or New York.
The point is that if the railways had done what the hon. member for St. John-Albert suggested they should do, then Canada would have lost the whole trade and would not have

had even the freight revenue consequent upon the carrying of the commodities to Portland.
I come now to the matter of the equalization of the rate to Portland. It should be clearly understood that the railway freight adjustment was not a matter of setting up discriminatory rates but of restoring equality. What must never be forgotten is that the Canadian railways are compelled to haul traffic to eastern ports at relatively low ton-mile revenue because of the longer mileages involved. For instance, here are the mileages from Montreal:

With this additional mileage involved, the railways cannot justify lower rates to Canadian ports than to the nearer United States ports. In effect the argument of the hon. member is that, on the eight or ten commodities referred to, the rates should be maintained on a lower basis than to the United States ports. If that suggestion were adopted, why should not all rates be similarly treated? Government policy never contemplated such a situation and it would be dangerous so to interpret it. If the Canadian railways had reduced the rate to United States ports below that applicable to Canadian ports the present complaint of the hon. gentleman would be well founded, but that is not the case. Where then has there been a violation of the traditional and historic policy of this country to encourage Canadian trade and the movement of Canadian trade via Canadian ports?
I should next like to deal with the question of French rye. There might- be a contradiction in these two terms, but the charge has been made by the hon. gentleman that the officials of the Canadian National Railways permitted a strangely inaccurate statement to be made by the manager of the French supply council and did nothing to encourage the movement of the rye through Canadian ports. So far as I am aware, the shipment of rye through Portland by the French supply council has no connection with nor was it in any manner influenced either by the shifting of Moore-McCormack sailings or by the reduction in the freight rate.
The hon. member considered it advisable to go into this matter at some length and to leave an inference, entirely unsupported, that some sinister influence operated on the part of Canadian officials to deflect this traffic from Canadian ports to Portland. I have made numerous inquiries, and all that I can find from the sources available to me is that the

The Address-Mr. Chevrier
Portland routing was the decision of the French supply council and the decision of that council alone. In the first place, I am advised by the officers of the Canadian National Railways that the traffic came to them with the routing definitely determined and established and stipulated by the shipper as to where it should go.
I am further advised by the officers of the national harbours board that at no time prior to the routing was this traffic discussed with them and that it is inconceivable that anyone connected with either the harbour of Halifax or the harbour of Saint John would have given Secretary General Hommey of the French supply council such palpably incorrect information as he is supposed or alleged to have given to the press. In the circumstances, the inference is left with me that whatever consideration influenced the decision the routing was fixed by the French authorities without inquiry from responsible sources as to the ability of Canadian ports to handle this business.
At this juncture I should like to say one word about the delegation which called to see me in connection with these matters.
