I have listened with interest to the minister's declaration of policy with regard to freight rates and transport in Canada, and now I should like to exercise my prerogative in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne to turn my attention to matters of defence in Canada. I am sorry that the minister is not in the chamber at the moment, but might I request his colleague the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) to draw his attention to the remarks I have to make this afternoon. I consider it appropriate that the Minister of Labour should be asked to do this, because I have expressed admiration for his declaration on a defence policy in Canada when he said that if you are not prepared to defend that which you have you will lose it.
On this occasion I have the honour to speak for my party on the subject of air defence of Canada. Though all of the things I might recommend would not, of course, be their responsibility, the views I shall put forward this afternoon have been endorsed by the defence committee of the Progressive Conservative party, and at the special request of our chairman, the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), I have been asked to put the case for air defence this afternoon, because we consider it to be a priority requirement in Canada.
I should like to mention one or two things that have been said in the past by men whom we all respect. The first one I wish to quote from is General Marshall in his report on the armed forces of the United States following world war II. He said, in referring to the United States:
We may elect again to depend on others, and the whim and error of potential enemies, but if we do we will be carrying the treasure and freedom of this great nation in a paper bag.
I contend that the quotation from General Marshall which I have just given is equally applicable to -our Dominion of Canada, because
ms
The Address-Mr. Skey

the defence needs of Canada and of the United States are completely interwoven. If one is threatened, so is the other.
Our Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), speaking in Montreal as recently as February 9, is reported by the Canadian Press as having said that it was impossible to rule out the possibility 'of aggression after looking at the Russian record in the field of international relations since the war.
We have General Marshall, who is so prominent today in trying to keep the peace, and our own minister saying that we must preserve our freedom by being prepared to defend it. I do not feel that I need labour these points any longer.
When I have spoken previously on this subject in the house I have recommended the air force as the most powerful of offensive weapons and the most effective defensive weapon. To illustrate this, the skilled German generals after the last war, when they were asked how we invaded the continent of Europe, paid our air forces the compliment of saying that they were the decisive factor, both in securing the invasion of Normandy and in the Germans' failure to contain that invasion. I have mentioned that previously in the house.
I have also spoken of the manpower situation and urged a survey of our manpower so that we might know what forces the country could sustain. I have spoken for air cadet training and called attention to the importance of cadet training in the schools and high schools of our country. I have called the attention of the house to the necessity of dual forces in Canada, equally balanced to defend our west and east, pointing out that we require a duplication in our defence needs. I have spoken about the great service rendered to all Canada's armed forces by the women of our country, by the Canadian girls who went into the navy, army and air force, and I have urged that their fine service be continued by enlisting them in reserve units. I have spoken also of supplementing our sendee personnel with civilian employees to increase the effectiveness of the few men we are able to enlist in our services today.
There is one subject, however, on which I have not had1 a great deal to say, but which I wish to discuss this afternoon, and that is the Canadian flying clubs. Prior to the war, Canadian flying clubs were paid a small subsidy for every trained pilot. I understand that now their costs have risen to a great extent. In the Toronto club they have risen from $900 to $2,200 a month, and they are

meeting there to discuss the possibility of washing up all their activities. I think it would be a great pity if Canada were to lose the services of the flying clubs which, from coast to coast, played such a great part in the formation of our defence forces in world war II. I urge the government to reconsider the adoption of the policy which they had prior to the war, namely, that of paying to these clubs some subsidies for those pilots whom they are able to train to a licence standard.
In addition to these considerations, we should be concerned at the present time with the production of our own aircraft in this country. In a recent editorial in Aircraft and Airport of December, 1947, I notice the following:
That Canada can build aircraft-good aircraft and lots of them-was proven in the not too distant past, but that vast potential built out of a wartime necessity has been allowed to dissipate and go down the drain with the fine phrases and rose-tinted promises made to the boys who came back.
We are faced today with an aircraft industry which is on the point of disintegration, and I suggest that we should do all we can to support it, so that machines may be built which our forces and civilian pilots will fly, in order to preserve for our country this great technical industry.
We are not the only country that is concerned with this industrial problem. The United States secretary for air, Mr. Symington, recently brought down a report. Although I have endeavoured to obtain an original copy, they are not available in Ottawa, and I must use the report from Time magazine of January 19, 1948, in giving the house a short resume of what the United States secretary for air had to say. In reporting on the industry, the commission pointed out, among other things:
A nation in the modern world is only as strong as the industry which produces its weapons. If air power was the nation's first line of defence-
I pause to call to the attention of the house the fact that this United States committee did find that air power was their first line of defence. I continue:
-it was a very weak line indeed, considering the state of the aircraft industry.
That is, of the industry in the United States.
Recently we have imported into Canada some fine, first-class jet fighter aircraft. I understand that members of the house will have an opportunity of examining some of them tomorrow. I feel that they are a step forward, but not the complete step until we are able to produce in our own country or at

The Address-Mr. Skey
least on this continent these machines, so that we shall have our forces supported by an integrated industry and not in the position in which they would be reinforced over long and precarious lines of communication.
In past years there has been some discussion in the house about the necessity of building up a proper intelligence and information service. I would certainly endorse this effort on the part of all Canada's armed forces. But with all these, the real strength of your defence forces lies in scientific research. I should mention the incorporation of a national research council member on the defence council of Canada. I think that is a forward step, and I believe that the representative selected is a fine and able man who will give real support and understanding to the needs of our armed forces.
I have said these things, Mr. Speaker, without political bias. There is. in truth, nothing in my speech that is with political bias, because I merely speak for what I believe to be the good of our country, for the protection of our people and for the protection of those social gains that we have been able to make under our system of government. Without the defence and security provided by our armed forces, the benefits of pensions, health insurance, medical clinics, mothers' allowances, and so on, can mean nothing, if we are vulnerable to the destructive force and fury of aggressive powers.
It may look as if I am standing here advocating the widespread use of the taxpayers' dollars. I am not doing that, however, because I propose to prove in the next few minutes that what I am advocating is the cheapest and best method of defending our country. The air force is peculiarly adapted to give us security and the most adequate defence with the maximum flexibility, which means that the smallest numbers can be used over the largest front. It is peculiarly suited to our geographic needs. It is a medium in which Canadians in two wars have proved themselves to be well skilled and able to compete, yes, more than compete, with the men of other countries. We have the great records of those who flew in the first world war. and we had our great training plan in Canada as a result of which forty or more squadrons of our men served in the front line in Europe and indeed across the world in the last war. When I mention this, I should like to call the minister's attention to an editorial in the Globe and Mail, dated Thursday, February 5, entitled, "Air power Canada's weapon". Set out there is, I believe, the most complete and able statement that I have seen
on the defence of Canada, and in particular the air defence of Canada, up to the present time. I quote in part from it as follows:
Relying as we undoubtedly do on this assistance-
That is, assistance from the United States. -we have a clear obligation to be ready with our own contribution to joint defence, one which suits our resources in manpower, skill and money. It needs no argument to prove that this contribution should be an air force larger and better equipped than the one we now have. It happens that such a force, besides being within our reach, provides the kind of defensive and striking power especially needed in a country of Canada's size and geography.
I believe the truth of those words is selfevident. I have some other quotations I could read on that point, but I think I can leave it, since it is so well stated by that editorial writer. It is indeed the cheapest defence we can buy, and the most effective at the present time. I will give the house just one illustration. During world war II, Britain had around her coasts a chain of early warning stations, which were able to plot the enemy bomber and fighter squadrons as they flew against the British isles. These stations gave good protection; when the German commanders estimated the fighter defences of the British isles they believed that the fighter force which opposed them was ten times greater than it actually was. In other words, by the application of the early warning service to the air force a small force was made ten times more effective. A few squadrons were as useful as many wings and groups would have been without it. Canada can make use of this great discovery and apply it economically to its own defence. Most emphatically it can, because during the last war Canadian technicians became especially skilled in the use of radar. We have heard the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) speak of its benefits to the merchant shipping. At the great school at Clinton, Ontario, we developed technicians who went not only to the Canadian forces but to all the allied forces, to show them the application of radar to the air weapon. This school was commanded by Wing Commander Patrick, who is now with RCA-Victor, and who during his time with the air force I believe made a unique contribution to his service and his country. Fortunately his good work has been continued by able successors, and I am pleased to learn that this great school at Clinton is carrying on into the peace, to use this great scientific device for the benefit of our service and the protection of our people. I might just make passing reference to the fact that this school is
The Address-Mr. Skey

in Huron county, where one of my service colleagues is contesting a by-election in a few days. I refer to Flight Lieutenant Tommy Pryde, who served with the army and air force in the first great war and with the air force in the last war. Even if he did not belong to my political party, he certainly would have my every sympathy. I am pleased to see, however, that his great record of national and community service is such as to recommend him to the people there over and above party considerations.
To change the theme of this address for a moment, I have already ventured the opinion that an adequate and reasonably balanced air force, balanced in content and supported by the devices of modern science, can give Canada the best defence protection at the present time. I now urge the government to adopt a policy in support of the R.C.A.F. which will develop it into a first-line defence force. I do not believe a country of the size and population of Canada can afford to be strong in all three services at the same time. Therefore, without apology, with great deference to and appreciation of the service rendered by our soldiers and sailors in the last war, and without detracting from that service in any way, I urge this policy upon the government.
I now return to another section of the report of Mr. Symington, secretary for air in the United States, in order to point out what was found by this commission appointed by the president. Here are some of their findings:	firstly, that the United States of
America is under definite threat. I shall not elaborate on that; but, if it is true, Canada is also threatened. Secondly, they also assume that any attack on democracy would be directed against the United States and that it would come without warning; thirdly, that the objective of any potential enemy would be the destruction of the United States, capacity to resist; fourthly, that security lay in keeping an air force in being in peace time greater than any other self-governed people have ever kept; fifthly, that neither minding one's business nor trying to reach a pacific accord among nations was enough at the present time. It is a pretty dismal prospect, and only because of that fact did I choose to speak on a subject which I know is unpopular, which may lead some people to attack me as a militarist and which is perhaps not foremost in the minds of the Canadian people at the present time.
Our military leaders, from George Washington to General Eisenhower, supported as recently as November 4 by Canada's General

Crerar, have urged a policy of peace through strength. Though we may all respect Mr. Ramsay MacDonald and his stand following world war I; while we may have admired him personally, we now know that he was wrong. On November 4, in New York, General Crerar said:
Until this -world of ours reaches a much higher plane of civilization and international understanding, I consider it essential that these countries which believe in the maintenance of peace, and in the arbitration or judicial settlement of international disputes which may endanger that condition, should be militarily prepared immediately and strongly to act in support of these principles.
Two days before that statement was made, General Marshall had reported that fifteen milliou men perished in world war II.
If I were to make recommendations, I should make reference, first, to several statements made in Montreal on February 9, by the Minister of National Defence. Firstly, he said that Canada cannot afford to maintain a huge peacetime defence force. Secondly, he said that we must ensure positive security under our own arms; thirdly, that we should co-operate with the United States and the commonwealth and, fourth, that our forces should be capable of rapid expansion. With those four statements I can have no quarrel. I consider that they are all sound, and that the only unsound feature is that we continue to spread the small amount we have for our defence forces, rather than to concentrate it on something that could be considered effective by way of an air defence force.
I would urge that he set up the type of force which could meet these immediate requirements, an air force which would be supported by adequate reserves, a force which would be highly trained and flexible, and provided with the most modern weapons and scientific assistance available.
Before concluding, I should like to refer to some of the more general aspects of the subject of defence. In this connection I should like to refer to a comment by Trygve Lie, secretary of the united nations, in London on January 29. He said the united nations had kept the peace for two years. The remark struck me forcibly because, much as we may hope for it, the united nations still remains an organization without any constables or magistrates to support its force.
Just a lot of truant officers.

Yes. And though we all admire the great work Mr. Lie has done, we wonder at his saying that the united nations has kept the peace for two years. His observation

The Address-Mr. Isnor
recalls to my mind, or to the mind of any thoughtful person, the speech made by Mr. Winston Churchill almost two years ago at Fulton, Missouri. Mr. Churchill then recommended that the united nations should receive the support of squadrons of aircraft, because they were the cheapest and most flexible armed unit, and that they could support the moral decisions of the constables and magistrates in this shrinking world. On that occasion Mr. Churchill said:
We must start immediately to equip the united nations with sheriffs and constables in the form of an armed force of air squadrons directed by the world organization.
Then he closed with these words:
. . . because our supreme task and duty is to guard the homes of the common people from the horrors of another war.
He thought only of peace; and who should think more of it than a man of his stature, who saw Britain at her weakest and her greatest during the days of the last war. I fully agreed with what he advocated at that time, and I repeated it in the house. What he said proved to be right.
Just a few days ago he rose in the British House of Commons to say that we must find a way to live with Russia during the next two years. The searching truth of his statements during the war, and of his appreciation at Fulton, Missouri, makes one apprehensive; because this man, when he speaks, does not speak carelessly. He speaks with the greatest of knowledge and says we have to find that solution within two years. The time factor is important-vitally important-in the world today.
I therefore say that, although we cannot afford to leave our people undefended at this time, we must redouble our diplomatic, political and social efforts to find a way to avert war, and to make unnecessary speeches such as I am making this afternoon. We must secure the peace and continue toward a realization of the four freedoms by all men, and the relief of our people from the remotest possibility of another conflict. While we may make these efforts for peace, we must support our armed forces and provide adequate protection for the Canadian people.
Mr. GORDON B. ISNOR (Halifax): Mr. Speaker, I rise because of a statement made today by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). However, before replying to or making comment in reference to those statements. I wish to add my support to what has been said by the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Hazen) in bringing to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and the government the, shall I say,
lack of efficiency or lack of interest shown by the officials of the Canadian National Railways in respect of shipments through maritime ports, namely Halifax and Saint John.
I am not going to cover the points discussed by the hon. member for St. John-Albert who, I think, laid the case for the maritimes before the minister in a strong, able and efficient manner. If what was said served no other purpose, at least it brought the minister to his feet today to place on record the facts relating to the equalization of freight rates between the ports of Halifax, Saint John and Portland.
While naturally I want to see every possible ton of cargo shipped through Halifax, if that is not possible, then my next thought would be that it should go through the other maritime port of Saint John, rather than through Portland. I wish only to add my sentiments in support of those of the hon. member for St. John-Albert.
I sat and listened to the hon. member for Cape Breton South when, as usual, he placed before the house a dreary and dismal picture of conditions in the maritime provinces, and particularly in his native province of Nova Scotia. He referred to the fact that I had given a statement to the press, and compared it with another statement. It appeared to me that he questioned the accuracy or the truth of what I said. I say to him that that statement was given in good faith, and I believe it to be correct. I am looking forward to the commencement, in the very near future, of the work I have mentioned.
I have had the co-operation of hon. members from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island in bringing about improvements in conditions in the maritimes. I resent, and I think many other hon. members will also, the thought thrown out by the hon. member for Cape Breton South that I was not willing to co-operate with other hon. members in working for the best interests of our province.
The hon. member said that hon. members should be careful as to the accuracy of their statements. I think that reference would apply more to the hon. member than to any other hon. member coming from the maritimes. I say that advisedly, after having listened to the hon. member on many occasions. I remember how he toured the county of Halifax during midsummer of last year along with some of his colleagues. I remember the extravagant statements which were made about the awful conditions in Nova Scotia, that we did not have any industry there, that nothing was going on, that there was no employment, that our farms were run down and so on. His col-
The Address-Mr. Isnor

leagues from the prairie provinces who were down there spoke along similar lines, but they did not dare go as far as the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
I think any hon. member who has had any business experience at all will realize that you cannot attract industry to a place which is always painted as being dead, dreary and dismal as has been done on more than one occasion by the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
How did it get that way?

I do not think it is that way. Perhaps I had better give the hon. member some information. I am glad to know that he couples himself with the hon. member for Cape Breton South by saying that it is that way.
What about housing in Halifax?

The hon. member who has just interrupted me is forever harping on housing, but I have yet to hear him offer anything constructive to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) in the time he has been here.
Are you proud of your Halifax houses?
I am just as proud of our Halifax houses as I am of the hon. member.
I know you do not think much of me.

I hope the hon. member is
ready to treat me with the same respect as I should like to treat him with, and I hope he will not interrupt me again. I feel I should answer him in regard to housing. Those hon. members who have kept in touch with the situation in Halifax realize that, prior to the war, we had a population of something like
60,000.	Because of the active part which Halifax took in the war effort, our population increased to around 135,000, and today it is around 95,000. I am ready to admit that our housing is not as it should be, but we are working toward an objective which will provide more houses for our people. We are not just talking about houses; we are making some constructive suggestions. At the present time there is under way a project which will provide five to six hundred houses. The contracts have already been let. There is another project in the offing which I hope will be under way within a month and which will provide another hundred houses. Those are concrete,

definite things, and I hope the hon. member will accept that as an answer to what he said about housing.
Then there is the $17,000,000; do not forget that.

The hon. member has always been ready to help me out. We are grateful to the Minister of Transport for showing the interest he has, not only in the great port of Halifax but also in the port of Saint John. In that connection I might say that we have definite assurance from the national harbours board that a new steel shed will be erected, at an estimated cost of $600,000, on pier 26 as soon as the steel is available. Plans and specifications have been prepared for the erection in a year's time of a modern concrete pier with two steel sheds. The existing pier is 600 feet long by 160 feet wide, and the proposed new pier, as planned at present, will be 700 feet long by 270 feet wide. The additional length will permit berthing two coastal size vessels on either side, whereas the present pier can accommodate only one on either side. It is estimated that the cost of this will be something like $3,900,000. Then there are other expenditures in connection with maintenance, totalling $246,000. In spite of all the unfair criticism that has been offered by the opposition, I think the Minister of Transport and the national harbours board are doing fairly well for Halifax.
Then a word as to the accuracy of statements. On more than one occasion the hon. member for Cape Breton South has referred to the closing down of the Trenton steel works and the unemployment that was created. For the benefit of the prairie members of the C.C.F., I should like to quote from the Eastern Chronicle of February 5, 1948, as follows:
Two major industries of Pictou county, the Eastern Car Company Limited and the Acadia Coal Company Limited continued their steady progress towards higher peaks of production, corporation figures tabulated for the month of January disclose.
An all-time record was set in the Eastern car shops, where the working force turned out fifty-ton boxcars at higher capacity per day than ever before experienced in the company's near forty-year history. Three hundred and eighty-six boxcars rolled from the assembly lines in January, all steel wood-lined, a number considerably greater than former figures on this type of construction. Some years ago, company officials said, wooden boxcars, i.e., unlined, were built faster than the current order is being handled, but the January, 1948, record exceeds the old wood type construction speed, in that the work involved on the present order greatly exceeds the old pattern.

The Address-Mr. Isnor
Seventeen hundred cars are being built by Eastern Car for the Canadian National Railways. with the end of the order scheduled for March.
I might mention for the information of the hon. member for Cape Breton South that in addition to these 1,700 cars, 250 seventy-ton hopper cars are being built, which order will run into something like $1,300,000 and will provide employment for a period of eight months. During the same midsummer period of last year, hon. members referred to the large lay-offs which had occurred in the Halifax dockyards. I regret that there were lay-offs in the Halifax dockyard, but I should like to place the actual facts before the house, so that they will realize that industry in Halifax is not completely run down. In 1939 there were something like 274 men on the payroll at the Halifax dockyard. During the war that number naturally increased, rising from 274 to 1,500, 2,000, 3,000 and up to 4,000. Then there was a drop, and the members of the C.C.F. went to Nova Scotia and told of the awful conditions in Halifax, of 500 employees being laid off today, 550 the next day, and so on. But actually today there are 1,890 employees on the payroll of the Halifax dockyard and they look to be fairly permanent. I mention that, Mr. Speaker, because of the effect which it is having on the rest of Canada and upon our province and particularly the city of Halifax of having men spread gloomy tales. You cannot build up if you are continually tearing down and belittling your own industries.
What I have said about the Halifax dockyard applies also to the adjacent shipyard. Not so many years ago we had the old Halifax Graving Dock Company there, employing from 150 to 250 men. Then came along what I consider was a real improvement, Halifax Shipyards Limited. They employed very large numbers of men, naturally, during the war doing ship repair work and constructing destroyers. I was interested in finding out the actual employment conditions in the Halifax shipyard, so I telephoned the general manager and asked him to be good enough to tell me the number of emplo3'ees on his payroll the previous month; that was about two months ago. I ascertained that there were 1.479 men employed at the Halifax shipyard, and at the subsidiary in Dartmouth, 374 men, or a total of 1.853, as against 250 or 300 employed years ago by the smaller company. That is the kind of figures the members of the C.C.F. never use. Instead, they use the lowest possible employment figure. In that way they do not, particularly the hon. member for Cape Breton South, do justice to their own part of the country, and that is to be regretted.
I believe I am speaking for the membership generally from the maritimes, irrespective of where they sit in this house, when I say that we regret that any one member should continually cry down his native province, as has been done for so long in this house. We recognize, of course, the fact that employment is not as good as it should be in our part of the country. We are not so situated as to enjoy markets such as they have in other parts of Canada. We have a population in Nova Scotia of around 600,000; in New Brunswick 500,000, and in Prince Edward Island, something like 100,000, or all told, a population of 1,200,000 for the maritime provinces, as against 4,500,000 to 5,000,000 in Ontario, concentrated around the large cities and furnishing, therefore, a readily available market for industrial production. But we still can brag of a certain number of industries in our province; and for the benefit of the hon. member for Cape Breton South I think I should give a few facts, so that he will have this information and perhaps use it in a different way from what he has been accustomed to doing in the past.
We have 1,281 industries in Nova Scotia, employing 38,000 men, paying wages of $60.000,000, and producing $204 million worth of goods. That may not be large in the eyes of members from Ontario, but to us it means something. Sixty million dollars in wages means a lot in a province of our size. Our manufacturers are shipping their goods to every part of Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific. We have one of the oldest coffee and spice firms, Schwartz, in our province, shipping its products right across Canada, from Halifax to Vancouver, and to the West Indies and overseas as well. We have Moir's chocolates, perhaps the finest chocolates sold in Canada today.
Mr. CRUICKSI-IANK: Any samples?
I feel sure that if they knew the desire of the hon. member for Fraser Valley they would be only too pleased to send him some.
Please see that they get that information.

I could go on for the benefit of my C.C.F. friends and tell them more about Nova Scotia. I could tell them that we have 33,000 farms in the province, notwithstanding that the members from the prairies who are farmers go down there and try to tell them how to make money and how it is possible to be successful when they are so unsuccessful themselves. Our farmers are still able to get a living
The Address-Mr. Isnor

off their farms. Our 33,000 farms maintain a population of 150,000. They produce 7,000,000 pounds of dairy butter, which is not bad for a small province. So I do not think we are so badly off in our province. We produce the finest apples grown in Canada, with a productive capacity of 2,000,000 barrels a year, the greater portion of which has in the past gone to the United Kingdom; but now that the whole of Canada has become acquainted with our apple juice, we are looking forward to markets for that product within Canada.
On motion of Mr. Isnor the debate was adjourned.
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Minister of Veterans Affairs if there is any possible chance of veterans legislation being brought into the house this week?

The resolution to set up the veterans affairs committee will appear on the order paper before the end of this week, and I can assure the hon. member that the legislation will be brought forward just as soon as possible thereafter.
